extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and current television comedy writers, especially those working in late-night/satirical news writers' rooms
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance on writing, editing, and managing jokes and segments for a late-night satirical news show (from a Daily Show head writer). Covers joke craft, host voice, room process, rehearsal-driven rewrites, and head-writer responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke supremacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The joke is always supreme: 'What is the smart thing to say in the funniest way possible?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize crafting jokes that are both smart and funny. The show's decision-making centers on whether a line is the right comic formulation of an idea rather than other considerations. Use humor that illuminates the idea as much as it amuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit with script/flow
rubrics_metrics.description: If a joke is really great but doesn't fit or confuses the script, then it's not worth keeping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate jokes for how they integrate into the piece's overall direction; during rewrite and rehearsal, cut otherwise-good jokes that disrupt tone, pacing, or clarity. The unitary thrust of a segment matters more than preserving isolated funny lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match the host's rhythm and voice
rubrics_metrics.description: There’s a rhythm—especially to Trevor’s humor and his style—that the show aims for every day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor jokes and phrasing to the host’s personal perspective, cadence, and sensibility. What works for one host (e.g., Trevor’s youthful, outsider viewpoint) may not work for another; maintain consistency with the host’s voice across a segment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think holistically as a head writer
rubrics_metrics.description: Head writing shifts focus from individual jokes to overall segment structure: 'Would this joke fit here? How would this joke work better? Could I change this to make the joke tighter?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a head writer, prioritize assignment, editing, and structural decisions rather than only writing lines. Consider placement, pacing between beats, and whether the segment allows space for a given joke; rework jokes to serve the piece's architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assigning and delegation process
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers are usually given a story and a headline; the head writer assigns stories and manages writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use morning and editorial meetings to decide stories and hand out assignments. Expect a workflow: morning meeting → assignments (~10:00am) → review (~11:30am) → continuing drafts and rewrites. Clear delegation and ownership speeds production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearsal-driven revision and rapid turnaround
rubrics_metrics.description: Rehearsal reveals what works and doesn’t; rapid rewrites occur in a small 'bunker' room shortly before taping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rehearsal feedback to identify riffs to keep, cut, or expand. Workers often have limited time (an hour or two) to produce a rehearsal draft and rework the script between meetings and taping. Project scripts, iterate collaboratively, and be prepared to rewrite quickly under time pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptability to breaking news
rubrics_metrics.description: Morning meetings confirm whether breaking news requires the show to change from the plan; the room pivots accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to abandon or adjust assigned pieces when a major news event occurs. Agile editorial decision-making early in the day prevents wasted work and keeps the show timely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize clarity and coherence over isolated cleverness
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s more important for the script to be clear and funny than to include a collection of disjointed jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When editing, favor coherence: a slightly less ambitious joke that serves the piece is better than a great joke that muddles meaning or interrupts flow. Use rewrite to align individual jokes to the piece’s intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative 'bunker' mentality
rubrics_metrics.description: The rewrite process is highly collaborative: writers, executive producers, and the host sit together and 'blast through jokes' projected on a wall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foster a fast, focused, collaborative environment late in the day where ideas are quickly tested, cut, or reshaped. Rapid group riffing and decisive editorial choices are central to polishing segments before taping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage personal obsessions/long-term watching as source material
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal obsessions (e.g., obsessively watching a show) can be turned into unique pieces and recurring bits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop storylines, character arcs, or recurring comedic premises from long-term attention to particular media or topics; such obsessions can yield original angles (example: 'I watch The Five' sketch built from watching a show repeatedly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialization and efficient process among writers
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers specialize in the show and develop efficient processes for producing material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate specialization—understanding the show's rhythms, recurring formats, and editorial expectations—to increase speed and quality. Institutional knowledge helps writers produce acceptable drafts quickly under daily production cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial collaboration with executive producers and host
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive producers and the host actively participate in reading drafts, giving notes, and sometimes writing parts themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect multi-level editorial input; be ready to incorporate notes from producers and the host. Collaboration often includes rewriting by multiple people and shared ownership of segments.
